A pause in the rhythm of life that had once included her, and now didn’t. My grandmother had died the winter before, and though time had moved forward, something in me had stayed behind. She wasn’t famous, but she was the kind of person who made ordinary things feel magical. The smell of cinnamon always takes me back to her kitchen, where she’d hum to herself while baking apple pies and telling stories about her childhood during the war. Her stories weren’t just words; they were spells that made the past come alive. Now, when I sat at the same wooden table, there was only the ticking of the clock and the faint smell of dust where cinnamon used to be. The first time I truly felt her absence was on my birthday: a day she had never once forgotten. Even in her final year, too frail to rise from bed, she had summoned the strength to send a hand-drawn card; the lines trembled with the weight of her illness, yet her familiar handwriting still breathed warmth and love. But that year, the letterbox remained silent.I stared at the blank space where her card should have been. It was an absence louder than any words. It was then I understood: grief doesn’t strike in grand gestures or singular moments; it seeps into the unnoticed corners of everyday life, settling into silence, into the pause where once there was presence. Sometimes I’d find myself picking up the phone, halfway to dialling her number before remembering. Other times, I’d dream about her, sitting in her favourite chair, gently correcting my grammar or telling me that my hair looked better the other way. I think I missed the way she made me feel more than anything—like I mattered, like I was enough just as I was. Without her, the world felt louder, more rushed and a little colder. Over time, the ache softened, but never entirely disappeared. I started baking her recipes, humming her tunes under my breath. Her memory became a fuzzy mix of warmth, comfort and something sad that I could never quite shake. *Your response will be marked for the accurate and appropriate use of vocabulary, spelling, punctuation and grammar.*
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer At first, it felt like flying. The rush of air, the sudden weightlessness, the illusion of freedom. For a brief second, I was soaring — suspended between sky and ground, between bravery and stupidity. Then came the landing. Sudden. Sharp. Final. And all that illusion shattered in an instant. It had started as a dare. A rusty footbridge stretched across the dried-up canal near the edge of the woods; the kind of place we weren’t supposed to go, which made it irresistible. We’d been there a dozen times, throwing stones, making dares, pretending we were wilder than we were. That afternoon, the sky had a strange golden haze and everything felt a little too still, like the moment before a storm. “Bet you won’t cross it,” Josh said, his voice casual but his eyes locked on mine. I laughed, too loudly, and began to climb. Inside, my stomach twisted, but I ignored it. I was fifteen. Pride mattered more than instinct. The wood was soft underfoot, splintering in places. Rusted nails jutted out like warning signs. Below me, the cracked canal floor was littered with rocks and broken glass. I told myself I’d be fine. That I had balance. That I wasn’t scared. But my hands trembled as I took each step. Then a board gave way, suddenly, sickeningly, and I fell. The world flipped. The sound was sucked out of the air. And then: the impact. I came to with a blinding bolt of pain screaming up my leg and a strange metallic taste in my mouth. My left side was scraped raw. My leg was twisted at an angle no leg should ever bend. I didn’t scream. I could not. I just stared at the sky, at the drifting leaves, thinking how quiet the world felt in that moment — like it had paused to take in what had happened. Josh was shouting my name, scrambling down, his voice cracking as he called for help. I remember gripping a patch of weeds, trying to anchor myself to something real. Not because I thought it would help, but because I did not know what else to do. The hours that followed blurred into colourless shapes: sirens wailing through the trees, paramedics cutting my jeans, my mother’s face pale with shock at the hospital. But what I remember most wasn’t the pain or the panic. It was the guilt. Guilt that I hadn’t listened to my gut. Guilt that I’d risked everything just to prove I wasn’t afraid. That fall hadn’t just broken my leg; it had fractured my sense of who I thought I was. I’d always believed I was careful. Thoughtful. But there, on that bridge, I had become someone reckless. Someone desperate to belong. Recovery was long: weeks confined to bed, a cast encasing my leg from hip to ankle, and crutches that left deep bruises along my arms.Yet, in time, my body mended, as it was designed to. What proved far more arduous was the process of forgiving myself. I realised, slowly, that the real fall was never physical. It was the fall from confidence, from certainty. And maybe, in a way, that fall was necessary. Because only by falling do we learn how to get back up. Now, I still pass that bridge sometimes. It’s cordoned off now, too unsafe even for dares. But I always stop for a moment, just to look. Not in fear, but in respect. It marks the place where I changed. Ellie and I had been best friends since we were five years old, when she shared her packet of crisps with me on the first day of school after seeing me sitting alone. From that moment, it was as if the world shifted slightly to fit us together. Two halves of one whole. We grew up side by side: climbing trees, sharing secrets whispered under blankets at sleepovers, laughing until our stomachs ached. At fourteen, we made matching bracelets from old ribbons and promised we’d be best friends forever. It felt unbreakable. But time has a way of testing promises. When we started sixth form, things changed. Ellie joined the hockey team, made new friends: confident, glamorous girls who spent their weekends at parties I was never invited to. I tried to tell myself it didn’t matter. We still met at the café after school sometimes, still messaged late at night. But it wasn’t the same. One afternoon, I waited for Ellie at our usual table by the window. I watched the rain trace tiny rivers down the glass, checked my phone again and again. No reply. She had promised she’d come. Finally, just as I was about to leave, I saw her rush in. She was laughing, drenched in the rain, surrounded by her new friends. Our eyes met across the room. She hesitated. For one fragile second, I thought she’d come over. But then one of the girls tugged her arm, pulling her into a booth and Ellie let herself be swept away. I stood there, invisible. That night, lying in bed, I thought about all the moments we’d shared. The time we got lost in the woods, the time we stayed up all night talking about our dreams. I wondered if she remembered them the way I did, if they still mattered. The next day, Ellie texted: Sorry I missed you. Things have just been crazy. Let’s catch up soon. I stared at the glowing screen for what felt like an eternity, the words blurring as my mind spun through a thousand memories. Finally, I typed back: Sure, let me know when. My finger hovered over the send button, trembling slightly, before I pressed it. I knew, deep down, that something indefinable had already slipped away. In that quiet, aching moment, a truth settled over me like a heavy blanket: friendship is not always about clinging desperately to what it once was. Sometimes, it is an act of quiet courage. It is recognising when to release your grasp, when to offer the freedom to change and evolve, even if it means accepting the painful reality of drifting apart. To love someone as a friend, I realised, is also to let them go. I think we shall always remain the truest of friends, though no longer in the manner we once were. I did not tell anyone where I was going. I left a note on the kitchen counter, scribbled quickly: "Gone walking. Back before dark." I zipped my coat, packed a flask and set off. The path I followed cut through a quiet stretch of woodland. The trees arched above me like the ribs of some ancient cathedral. Sunlight streamed between the branches and I let myself breathe more deeply than I had in weeks. Every footstep felt steady, measured. The world seemed calm and reliable. But only for a while. By the time I realised how far I had walked, the sky had started to shift. The light thinned and a mist began to creep through the trees. At first it was delicate, almost beautiful, blurring the edges of the path like soft pencil smudges. Then it thickened. Soon, the trees were gone, swallowed by the distance. I turned back, or at least I thought I did. But every tree looked identical. Every direction seemed unfamiliar. My hands began to shake as I pulled out my phone. No signal. The compass app spun meaninglessly. I quickened my pace, hoping to retrace my steps. The faster I walked, the less certain I became. Branches clawed at my arms and damp leaves clung to my boots. My breath came shorter now, not from exertion but from panic. Then I tripped. One moment I was upright, the next I was sprawled in the undergrowth. My head slammed against something solid and a burst of pain exploded behind my eyes. I lay still for a moment, dazed and half expecting the forest to swallow me whole. The cold nipped at my cheeks. My lip was bleeding. But slowly, I pulled myself upright. I didn’t know which way to go, only that I could not stay where I was. I walked again, this time more cautiously. Then I saw it. A scrap of red caught on a branch ahead. My scarf. I remembered it slipping from my neck earlier. My heart pounded as I reached for it. I was not safe yet, but I had found something familiar. I had watched her make lasagne dozens of times. It looked simple enough: pasta, meat, sauce, cheese. What could possibly go wrong? I assembled the ingredients proudly. I even made a playlist to set the mood, something upbeat and Italian-sounding. Within minutes, I had minced beef sizzling in the pan, onions softening, and garlic filling the kitchen with that impressive, chef-like smell. I felt invincible. Then came the white sauce. Or, more accurately, the floury mess that resembled white sauce only if you squinted and lowered your expectations. I whisked it with determination, ignoring the lumps and telling myself that no one really noticed sauce texture anyway. I layered everything into the dish like I’d seen on TV, sprinkled grated cheese with flair, and placed it in the oven with the satisfaction of a seasoned cook. That’s when I noticed the empty packet of lasagne sheets. And that’s when it hit me. I had forgotten to cook the pasta. Apparently, the phrase "oven-ready" on the packet does not mean you can ignore it entirely and hope for the best. Still, by the time I realised, the lasagne was already bubbling in the oven and the top looked golden and delicious. I convinced myself it might be fine: maybe the sauce would soften the pasta. Maybe it would be rustic. Or authentic. Or chewy in a charming way. It was not. When Mum came home and we all sat down to eat, I served up generous slices and waited proudly for their reactions. My brother took one bite, frowned, and then tried to saw through a sheet of pasta that had all the flexibility of reinforced concrete. Mum smiled politely, which is her way of saying, “I’m trying not to laugh, but this is inedible.” I admitted it. “I didn’t cook the pasta sheets.” There was a long pause. Then, to my surprise, Mum burst out laughing. My brother joined in. I laughed too, though part of me wanted to hide in the cupboard with the last of the grated cheese. I had just settled into the armchair with a book I’d read too many times before, comforted by its predictability, when the doorbell rang. Once. Then again. From the outset, the saw is given a threatening, almost living presence: Frost describes how it “snarled and rattled” using violent verbs that suggest aggression and danger. This makes the boy seem powerless in comparison, especially as he is not even mentioned until later, which builds a sense that he is insignificant compared to the dangerous machinery he works with. Furthermore, the use of onomatopoeia “snarled” and repetition “snarled and rattled, snarled and rattled”, emphasises the menace of the saw and foreshadows the terrible disaster that follows. Frost further builds sympathy for the boy by showing how young and innocent he is. He is only referred to as “the boy” which distances him from the adult world and reminds the reader of his youth. Despite his young age, he is “Doing a man’s work” making the reader pity his loss of childhood. His longing for a break, “Call it a day, I wish they might have said”, shows how much he wishes to escape his adult responsibilities and to give him “the half hour/That a boy counts so much when saved from work.” When the accident happens, the moment is both sudden and shocking: “At the word, the saw... Leaped out at the boy’s hand”. Frost’s language personifies the saw, making it seem as if it acts with a will of its own, further reinforcing the boy’s helplessness. His initial response, a “rueful laugh”, shows his shock and denial. Sympathy for the boy increases when he raises his injured hand, “Half in appeal, but half as if to keep / The life from spilling”, which conveys his instinct to survive and his sudden awareness of mortality. His plea, “Don’t let him cut my hand off— / The doctor, when he comes. Don’t let him, sister!” is tragic, as the reader knows it is already too late. The fact that the narrator is unsure where the cry is coming from and even questions his own hearing by saying “Nothing” builds unease. He wonders whether he is hearing “some long-dead ghost” which suggests a supernatural presence and immediately raises the tension. His plan to comfort himself by going to make a drink and stir up the fire only increases this tension because the reader senses that something more threatening is about to occur. ### Model answer In ‘The Bright Lights of Sarajevo’, Tony Harrison presents war as a destructive, dehumanising force that affects every part of daily life. Through the poet’s vivid description of violence and hardship, contrasted with the gentle, almost romantic behaviour of the young people, the poem explores how conflict shapes a city but does not fully erase the humanity of its people. The writer uses structure and imagery to convey both devastation and resilience. The poem opens by focusing on the practical impact of war on everyday life. People are shown as struggling to survive: they queue for gas “to get the refills they wheel home in prams” and carry “meagre grams / of bread” up “sometimes eleven flights / of stairs”. These images present war as physically exhausting and emotionally draining. The use of progressive tense verbs like “queuing”, “dodging” and “struggling” conveys the daily, ongoing difficulty faced by the people of Sarajevo. These challenges are not temporary moments of hardship, but part of an extended routine. The poem also highlights the sense of danger that lingers in public spaces. Although we are told that “you’d think that the nights / of Sarajevo would be totally devoid / of people”, the city is not empty. This contradiction suggests surprise that people are still choosing to go out, despite the risk. The phrase “streets Serb shells destroyed” implies a background of violence and destruction and there is a quiet horror in the mention of people dodging snipers just to get water or bread. Even the sky, described as “ideally bright and clear for bomber’s eye”, seems threatening. The word “ideally” would usually have a positive connotation, but here it is used ironically to suggest that even a beautiful sky becomes dangerous during war. Despite this, Harrison introduces a contrast in tone through the description of young people walking the streets at night. He writes that they move “at a stroller’s pace”, which is surprising given the violent context. This relaxed rhythm suggests a quiet resistance or resilience. The phrase “black shapes impossible to mark / as Muslim, Serb or Croat in such dark” presents the darkness not just as a physical condition, but also as a symbolic equaliser. It removes the divisions that led to conflict. The poet seems to admire the way these young people reclaim the streets through peaceful acts like flirting, walking and holding hands. There is a sense of hope and connection in the way the couple are described. The boy is guided by the “tender radar of the tone of voice” and tries to check “in her eyes if he’s made progress yet”. These intimate details reflect a kind of innocent romance that feels out of place against the war-torn setting. The couple are seen standing “on two shell scars”, which marks the very spot where people were “massacred” while queuing for bread. The contrast between love and violence is most powerful here. The use of “blood-dunked crusts of shredded bread” creates a grotesque image of everyday food turned into a symbol of suffering. Yet above the same spot, a boy and a girl fall in love. The structure of the poem supports this contrast. Harrison starts with images of suffering and ends with the couple sharing “one coffee in a candlelit café” and walking away “behind AID flour sacks refilled with sand”. This final image captures both the ongoing threat of war and the attempt to preserve ordinary life. The sacks are meant for aid, but are now used for defence, symbolising how even help becomes part of the fight for survival. The candlelit café evokes warmth, comfort and normality, showing how people find meaning even in the bleakest of circumstances. The contrast between the romantic metaphor and the source of the puddles, “Serb mortar shells”, emphasises how war distorts even the most innocent moments. ### Model answer In ‘Disabled’, Wilfred Owen presents a powerful and tragic portrait of a young soldier who has been physically and emotionally broken by war. Through contrasting descriptions of the soldier’s past and present, as well as vivid sensory language, Owen explores how war has stripped him of his youth, purpose and dignity. The poem uses structure, imagery and voice to evoke deep sympathy for the soldier, portraying him as isolated, regretful and forgotten. The poem opens by presenting the soldier in a state of physical and emotional decline. He is described as sitting “in a wheeled chair, waiting for dark,” which immediately suggests passivity, helplessness and a life without joy. The phrase “waiting for dark” has a double meaning, referring both to nightfall and possibly death. The use of colour imagery such as “ghastly suit of grey” reinforces the lifelessness of the soldier’s present, as does the chilling verb “shivered”. In contrast, the voices of children playing in the park are “saddening like a hymn,” suggesting that even the sounds of life and happiness around him now only deepen his sense of loss. Owen creates sympathy here by showing how the soldier feels completely removed from the world he once belonged to. In addition, Owen uses memories of the soldier’s past to heighten the tragedy of his present. The soldier recalls how “Town used to swing so gay”, evoking a vibrant social life filled with music, lights and romance. He remembers being admired for his looks, “There was an artist silly for his face,” and being carried “shoulder-high” after football matches, a symbol of physical strength and popularity. These joyful images are contrasted sharply with the soldier’s present condition: he is now legless, “sewn short at elbow” and women treat him like “some queer disease.” The use of contrast is one of Owen’s key techniques to evoke sympathy. The soldier’s vibrant youth is replaced by a cold, immobile present, where he is ignored by society and left alone. These shifts create deep sympathy by showing how drastically the war has altered the course of his life. The poet also presents the soldier’s decision to join the army as naïve and manipulated, which creates further sympathy. Owen writes that he joined because “he’d drunk a peg” and wanted to “please the giddy jilts” suggesting immaturity and impulsiveness. The soldier is shown to have been seduced by romanticised images of war: “daggers in plaid socks”, “smart salutes” and “Esprit de corps”. The repetition of these almost comical images reveals the gap between fantasy and the brutal reality he now faces. Owen writes, “Smiling they wrote his lie” emphasising that those around him encouraged or enabled his decision without fully considering the consequences. This creates a sense of injustice, as the soldier did not understand what he was truly signing up for. Owen’s use of structure and repetition also increases the reader’s sympathy. The poem ends with a return to the image from the beginning: “He sat in a wheeled chair, waiting for dark.” This circular structure reinforces the idea that nothing has changed for the soldier. His life is now a cycle of waiting, helplessness, and neglect. The final lines, “Why don’t they come / And put him into bed?” express a childlike desperation. The repetition of “Why don’t they come?” gives the impression of someone abandoned and powerless, entirely dependent on others. This closing question leaves a lasting emotional impact, highlighting his loneliness and the complete loss of agency. Owen also uses poetic devices such as alliteration and enjambment to deepen the sense of pity and to highlight how the soldier is treated before and after he is injured. The poetic rhythm contrasts the freedom and movement of the past with the static, trapped existence of the present in which he is shown pity or forgotten. parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer Kate Chopin presents marriage in The Story of an Hour as a deeply complex and, at times, repressive institution, particularly for women like Mrs. Mallard. Through Mrs. Mallard’s shifting emotions, including her initial grief, emerging joy, and eventual tragic end, Chopin explores the tension between love and personal freedom. She reveals how marriage can be both comforting and confining. At the beginning of the story, Mrs. Mallard’s immediate response to her husband’s reported death is consistent with what society expects of a devoted wife. She weeps “at once, with sudden, wild abandonment,” which implies emotional devastation and reinforces the idea that she loved her husband. However, the writer quickly complicates this image. The phrase “She did not hear the story as many women have heard the same” introduces the idea that Mrs. Mallard’s reaction will be different from societal norms. As she retreats alone to her room, a space of solitude and introspection, the tone begins to shift. Chopin presents the complexity of Mrs. Mallard’s true feelings about her marriage. Mrs. Mallard’s thoughts about her future reveal how marriage has stifled her sense of self. As she sits in her room, she experiences a “suspension of intelligent thought” and then, gradually, a transformation begins. Chopin uses natural imagery such as “patches of blue sky”, “the delicious breath of rain” and “sparrows” that were “twittering” to reflect Mrs. Mallard’s awakening to freedom. These positive and peaceful images represent the new life she envisions, a life free from the expectations and limitations of being a wife. When she whispers, “free, free, free!” it becomes clear that her grief is being replaced by a powerful sense of relief and possibility. The repetition of the word “free” and the short sentences build emotional intensity, suggesting that she has long felt imprisoned by her marriage. Despite her husband being described as having “never looked save with love upon her,” Mrs. Mallard acknowledges that “she had loved him — sometimes.” Chopin juxtaposes this tender memory with Mrs. Mallard’s exhilaration at her new independence, indicating that even a loving marriage may still be restrictive. The phrase “There would be no one to live for during those coming years; she would live for herself” highlights the theme of self-assertion. ### Model answer In Robert Frost’s poem ‘Out, Out —’, the writer creates strong feelings by presenting the tragic accident of a young boy in a way that is both shocking and emotionally powerful. Through vivid language, dramatic structure, and a blend of calm imagery with sudden violence, Frost evokes sympathy, disbelief and sadness in the reader. The poem explores how quickly life can be lost and how others may respond with a disturbing sense of detachment. The poem opens with a description of the buzz saw, which is presented as a threatening and almost living force. Frost uses personification to create a menacing tone: “The buzz saw snarled and rattled in the yard”. The repetition of “snarled and rattled” throughout the poem makes the sound aggressive, as if the saw is angry or alive. This foreshadows the danger that is to come. The power of the saw is further emphasised when Frost writes, “And made dust and dropped stove-length sticks of wood”, suggesting that it works with mechanical violence. Later, the poem describes how the saw “Leaped out at the boy’s hand, or seemed to leap—” which again personifies it and makes it feel like a predator. This gives the reader a sense of unease and sets up the emotional shock of the accident. Frost also builds a peaceful and calm setting before the tragedy, creating a painful contrast. He writes, “Five mountain ranges one behind the other / Under the sunset far into Vermont.” These lines are peaceful and almost idyllic, but they make the violence of the accident more sudden and horrifying. Frost continues this contrast with “day was all but done”, which suggests the ending of both the day and, symbolically, the boy’s life. The tone here feels like closure, which is then shattered by the tragedy. The accident itself is sudden and confusing. Frost writes, “He must have given the hand. However it was, / Neither refused the meeting.” This suggests uncertainty and shock, and the fact that the saw and hand are described as if they both agreed to the accident adds to the strange, surreal feeling. The moment is given extra emphasis through the short sentence, “But the hand!”, which powerfully shows how everything changes in an instant. This moment is deliberately fragmented to reflect the emotional impact. Frost presents the boy in a way that creates deep sympathy. He is described as a “big boy / Doing a man’s work, though a child at heart”, which highlights how he is still too young for the responsibility and danger of this task. The fact that he is interrupted from work by his sister saying, “Supper”, reminds the reader that this is still a domestic, childlike setting. His initial reaction, “a rueful laugh”, is shocking and sad, because it shows his disbelief. Then he tries to save himself, swinging toward the others “Half in appeal, but half as if to keep / The life from spilling”. These lines are full of emotion, as they show the boy’s fear and desperation. As the poem progresses, the horror increases. His plea, “Don’t let him cut my hand off— / The doctor, when he comes. Don’t let him, sister!” shows both his terror and his childish need for protection. Soon after, Frost writes, “The boy saw all— / Since he was old enough to know, big boy / Doing a man’s work”, which shows the boy’s realisation that his life has been ruined. The boy’s death is described with chilling simplicity: “Little—less—nothing!” This line, with its pauses and stark finality, creates a strong emotional impact. The people around the boy simply move on: “And they, since they / Were not the one dead, turned to their affairs.” This lack of emotion or mourning is shocking and creates a sense of coldness and detachment. It suggests that the boy’s death is quickly forgotten, which adds to the tragic mood. Harrison writes that they must wait in long queues “with empty canisters of gas” and carry “precious meagre grams / of bread” back home. These details suggest deprivation and hunger. The line “struggling up sometimes eleven flights / of stairs with water”, further emphasises how difficult life has become, especially when basic needs like water must be carried by hand. These images create sympathy in the reader, as they reveal just how exhausting and dangerous daily routines are. Danger is made even more clear in the line “dodging snipers on the way”, which shows that people are constantly at risk, even while doing ordinary things. Harrison then describes the streets as destroyed by “Serb shells”, painting a picture of a broken, war-torn city. However, in contrast to these images of fear and destruction, Harrison introduces a moment of unexpected normality and beauty: “tonight in Sarajevo that’s just not the case —” The shift from hardship to calm creates a powerful contrast. Despite everything, the young people still “go walking at stroller’s pace”, which gives a sense of peace and determination. Harrison uses the relationship between the young couple to represent a kind of hope and resistance. They are not described in detailed dialogue, but instead through physical movement: “the dark boy-shape leads dark girl-shape away”. The fact that they walk at night, without fear, and engage in gentle flirting shows that they have not allowed the war to take away their humanity. They are standing on the very spot where, in 1992, a “breadshop queue” was attacked by “Serb mortars”. ### Model answer In The Necklace, Guy de Maupassant presents money and possessions as symbols of social status, personal worth and ultimately, human folly. Through Madame Loisel’s obsession with wealth and appearance and the devastating consequences of a single lost item, the narrative explores how materialism can shape and ruin lives. From the beginning, the narrator shows that Madame Loisel is deeply dissatisfied with her modest circumstances. Though married to a junior clerk and in a comfortable house, she feels she was “intended for a life of refinement and luxury”. Maupassant describes her constant unhappiness and longing for possessions she cannot afford: “the peeling walls, the battered chairs, and the ugly curtains” torment her, where another woman of similar status might not even notice them. This shows that, for Madame Loisel, material surroundings are not just decorative, but they define her sense of identity and happiness. Madame Loisel’s dreams are rich with vivid imagery, reinforcing the importance she places on money and class. She imagines “tall, bronze candelabras”, “old silk” and “exquisite dishes served on fabulous china plates”. These ornate details contrast sharply with her actual life and indicate her desire to escape into a world of grandeur. Maupassant suggests that her dissatisfaction is not about need, but about perceived social worth; she doesn’t want to simply be comfortable, but she wants to be admired and envied. Through negative language and repetition, Maupassant further reinforces her dissatisfaction and longing. The phrase “no dowry, no expectations, no means of meeting some rich, important man” uses a tricolon to emphasise all that she lacks, setting a tone of deprivation from the outset. Similarly, the list “no fine dresses, no jewellery, nothing” underscores how utterly deprived she feels of the luxuries she believes she deserves. Her constant unhappiness is captured through the repeated phrase “all the time”, showing that thoughts of wealth dominate her daily existence. This desire for status is shown again when Madame Loisel receives an invitation to the Ministry Ball. Rather than being excited, she reacts with bitterness: “What earthly use is that to me?” The invitation is dismissed because she lacks the dress and jewellery to present herself as wealthy. This response highlights how possessions, for her, are necessary to be seen as valuable. Her husband’s practical view in suggesting that she wears flowers instead of jewellery is rejected, as she fears this would be “humiliating” among richer women. Similes and personification are also employed to depict poverty unflatteringly. When faced with the idea of attending the ball without jewellery, Madame Loisel protests, “I’ll look like a church mouse” equating poverty with insignificance. Even the hackney cabs in the street are described with shame, emerging only “after dusk, as if ashamed to parade their poverty in the full light of day”. These images heighten the humiliation and burden Madame Loisel associates with being poor. Maupassant uses the borrowed necklace as the ultimate symbol of how possessions can deceive and destroy. Madame Loisel borrows a diamond necklace from her wealthy friend, which gives her the confidence and joy she has long desired. At the ball, she is “elegant, graceful, radiant”, her beauty enhanced not by who she is, but by what she wears. However, when she loses the necklace, her life descends into “grim poverty” and “heavy domestic work”. The irony is that the necklace was a worthless imitation. This cruel twist reveals how her obsession with appearances led her to suffer needlessly for a symbol of wealth that had no real value. She behaves “peevishly”, “irritably” and responds “shortly”. In contrast, when she has the chance to possess luxury, even temporarily, her emotions shift dramatically. She opens the invitation “eagerly”, borrows the necklace “extravagantly”, and dances “wildly” and “ecstatically” at the ball. These contrasting adverbs reflect how her mood is shaped entirely by her relationship to wealth. In conclusion, The Necklace presents money and possessions not only as measures of social class but as powerful forces that shape identity, perception and destiny.
